name: US HOA, condo and co-op association assessments and capital repairs
geography: United States (Florida and California are the largest concentrations)
size_basis: FCAR 2025 Statistical Review (verified PDF): $124.2B of assessments collected in 2025, of which $31.1B contributed to reserve funds; 373,000 associations; 35.2% of US housing; 9,000-10,000 management companies; 30-40% self-managed; Florida 50,600 associations / 4.47M units.
money_flow: Owners pay assessments to associations, which pay management companies, insurers, utilities, landscapers and contractors, and fund reserves for roofs, elevators, structure and pools. Signers: board treasurer/president on owner votes (Florida allows loans and lines of credit with majority owner approval), advised by the management company.
shock: Fannie Mae Lender Letter LL-2026-03 (Mar 18, 2026): minimum reserve allocation rises from 10% to 15% of annual budgeted assessment income for loan applications dated on/after Jan 4, 2027; Limited Review ended for established projects >10 units (Aug 3, 2026 per summaries). Buildings that miss the floor lose conventional financing eligibility. Florida: reserves must be funded to 100% of structural-integrity study recommendations from Jan 1, 2026 with no waiver (HB 913, 2025); Miami Realtors found 62% of South Florida associations missed the original Dec 31, 2024 study deadline. Fannie PDF returned 403; five secondary summaries agree.
incumbents: Management companies (9,000-10,000 firms), reserve-study firms (Association Reserves, Reserve Advisors), portfolio banks that lend to associations (e.g. U.S. Century Bank in Miami), insurers writing master policies.
incumbent_fragility: 30-40% of associations are volunteer-run; boards face a hard compliance deadline with six-figure per-unit exposure in some Florida buildings; conventional unit-owner financing is tightening; association lending is bank-local and slow.
funded_startups_already_here: Vantaca (HOA management software, $300M+ growth round at $1.25B Oct 2025, Cove Hill Partners; 500+ management companies, 6M households); PayHOA ($27.5M Series A May 2024); Assembly HOA ($1.8M); Bluejay HOA ($2.0M). Found no venture-scale startup in association capital-project financing or procurement.
wedge_hints: Special-assessment financing and loan servicing for Florida condo associations (lien-secured); 15%-rule budget modeling and lender-eligibility reporting; milestone-inspection repair project procurement; master-policy premium financing.
insider_roles: Community association managers, reserve specialists, condo attorneys, association lending officers at community banks, engineers performing milestone inspections, insurance brokers placing master policies.

name: US building-permit plan review and inspection (government and private providers)
geography: United States (Florida, Texas, California, Tennessee lead on private-provider laws)
size_basis: My derivation: BLS counts ~133,640 construction and building inspectors (May 2023, mean wage $72,880) and ~147,600 jobs in 2024 (OOH, median $72,120) = ~$10-11B in inspector wages alone, excluding plan examiners, permit technicians, software, overhead and private-provider fees. Context: Census Aug 2026 private residential construction $882B SAAR, total $2.2T.
money_flow: Applicants pay permit, plan-review and inspection fees to cities and counties; under private-provider laws they pay licensed third-party reviewers/inspectors directly. Signers: builder/contractor permit coordinator or owner; city building official or CIO.
shock: State laws moving work to private providers when governments miss deadlines: Florida HB 803 (signed May 6, 2026, effective July 1, 2026) sets a 10-business-day clock with private providers (5 for single-trade single-family work), deemed approval on a miss, and reported 50% commercial permit-fee cut when private providers do all review and inspection; California AB 253 (signed Oct 10, 2025) allows third-party review after 30 days; Texas HB 14 (2023) and SB 1450 (2025); Tennessee Public Chapter 771 (2024); Florida HB 683 (2025).
incumbents: Municipal building departments, permitting-system vendors (Tyler Technologies, Accela, Clariti; vendors other than Clariti from background knowledge), code-consulting and third-party review firms.
incumbent_fragility: Public departments are understaffed and statutory clocks now shift volume to private providers faster than departments can hire; permit software vendors sell to the same governments losing volume.
funded_startups_already_here: PermitFlow ($54M Series B Dec 2025 led by Accel; ~$90M total); CivCheck (AI plan review, acquired by Clariti; Honolulu requires it for eligible residential projects from Sept 1, 2026; Denver uses it). No venture-backed licensed private-provider firm combining software and a state inspection license was found.
wedge_hints: Licensed private provider (plan review plus inspection) in FL/TX/CA/TN earning the review and inspection fee with software doing first-pass checks; single-trade permits (solar, HVAC, roofing, electrical) where the shortest clocks apply; inspection scheduling for builders.
insider_roles: Building officials, plan examiners, ICC-certified private providers, permit expediters, builder permit coordinators.

name: Gas-turbine fleet services and aftermarket (maintenance, repair, parts, upgrades, LTSAs)
geography: Global (US share ~$4.5B per GMI); the US fleet is central to the shock
size_basis: GMI (paid report): $27.1B in 2025 and $30.2B in 2026, US $4.5B. Other paid reports range $10-25B depending on scope (Future Market Report $10.25B; MarkNtel all-turbine services $25.3B in 2026, gas ~46%). Filing cross-check: GE Vernova's Power services revenue was $13.07B in 2025 (gas, steam, nuclear and hydro together; not split) against $6.42B of equipment. Siemens Energy Gas Services ~EUR 1.6B in FY2025 (unconfirmed whether revenue or profit). Treat as a $10-30B range, ~$30B at the top.
money_flow: Plant owners (utilities, IPPs, industrials, data-center BTM operators) pay OEMs through long-term service agreements (LTSAs), parts and outage services; independent service providers and repair shops take a minority (top 5 firms hold ~39% of global services per MarkNtel).
shock: GE Vernova's gas equipment backlog plus slot reservations rose from 100 to 116 GW in Q2 2026 (target >=125 GW by year-end), it is selling 2031 slots, and output is 20 GW/yr rising to 24 GW in 2028 and 30 GW in 2030. New heavy-duty units are unavailable for years, so owners must keep old frames running, defer retirements and lengthen overhaul cycles, while BTM data-center adds enlarge the fleet needing service.
incumbents: GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi, Solar/Baker Hughes, Ansaldo capture the money via LTSAs, proprietary hot-gas-path parts and outage services; a thin layer of independent service providers.
incumbent_fragility: OEMs prioritize scarce factory and field-service capacity for new equipment (business-model conflict with servicing old units cheaply); outage labor is short; parts lead times are long; owners have little price transparency on LTSAs. Proprietary designs lock parts, but also leave gaps where owners cannot get service slots.
funded_startups_already_here: None found focused on turbine MRO/parts after two broad searches (treat as open but confirm with named-company checks before building). Adjacent: ProEnergy (private) selling repurposed CF6 jet-engine cores for data-center power.
wedge_hints: LTSA and parts-price benchmarking and audit for owners; condition-based outage planning (borescope AI, digital twins); a certified marketplace for surplus frames, aeroderivatives and spare parts including slot transfers; outage-technician staffing and credentialing; rotable inventory pooling among IPPs and co-ops; independent hot-gas-path repair (capital intensive). Bottom-up sketch (assumption): benchmarking/audit at 1% of a ~$20B accessible pool is $200M but early capture is a fraction; surplus-equipment brokerage at 3-5% of a few $B/yr of trades reaches $100M+ only if scarcity persists.
insider_roles: Plant O&M directors at IPPs and utilities; outage managers; combustion engineers; LTSA contract managers; ex-OEM field service reps; independent service-provider shop owners; insurer engineering surveyors.

name: US OEM and prime purchases of metal castings from foundries (defense-critical)
size_basis: AFS (American Foundry Society, July 2026): US metalcasting industry revenue about $53.7B in 2025, with casting sales projected +8.0% in 2026 (about $58B), up from a 4.2% January projection [primary]. Forgings are not included; the only FIA figure found was $10.6B of custom-forging shipments in 2012, too old to use. Foundry count not found.
money_flow: OEMs and defense primes (valves and fittings, pumps, heavy equipment, vehicles, rail, aerospace and defense) pay foundries for castings; foundries buy scrap, alloys, sand and patterns and do their own finishing.
shock: The Department of War's Manufacturing Technology Program Strategic Plan FY2026-2031 (published 2026-09-30) names castings, forgings and microelectronics as single points of failure and states the department lacks latent capacity to rapidly scale production of key systems and munitions in a crisis, citing offshoring, consolidation, qualification delays and small-supplier financing gaps (no new dollars attached). A Pentagon acquisition official is quoted saying the defense cast-and-forge supply chain has shrunk 80% (date unclear), with at least 122,000 more workers needed by 2028. AFS puts tariff cost to the industry near $1B to date; a June 2026 MxD roadmap cites aging equipment and offshoring.
incumbents: Thousands of small and mid-size foundries; large aerospace casting and forging houses (Howmet, PCC, Wyman-Gordon, Carpenter, from memory). About 377 foundries make valves and pipe fittings (narrower count).
incumbent_fragility: Capital-intensive, environmentally permitted, aging workforce, long pattern and tooling lead times, and NADCAP/AS9100 qualification that takes months to years, so customers cannot easily dual-source and capacity is sticky and cannot flex to surge demand.
funded_startups_already_here: Fabri (MIT spinout, investment casting, $13.5M total, backed by RTX Ventures and Lockheed Martin Ventures, second foundry targeted for 2027; one profile dates a seed to 2026-06, likely a data artifact); Foundry Lab (New Zealand, microwave casting, $8M Series A, date unclear). Adjacent: Hadrian (CNC, not casting). No funded foundry-sourcing marketplace or qualification-as-a-service company found.
wedge_hints: Casting and forging sourcing and qualification (RFQ routing, first-article, NADCAP-ready paperwork); pattern and tooling as-a-service (digital twin, 3D-printed sand molds); foundry capacity and utilisation data; casting-to-machining kitted supply for primes; foundry roll-up with software. Bottom-up check: a 3% take on $53.7B is about $1.6B of flow-based revenue, so $100M needs about 6% of the pool at 3% take; needs trust and qualification credentials first.
insider_roles: Foundry owners, melt and pattern-shop managers; prime supplier-quality engineers; DCMA reps; NADCAP auditors; AFS and FIA staff; metallurgists qualifying alloys.

name: US health plans' and self-funded employers' out-of-network payments through No Surprises Act arbitration (IDR awards)
size_basis: About $15B of IDR payouts in 2025, more than triple 2024's $4.08B, per a WSJ analysis of CMS data (read via Healthcare Dive). Georgetown/Health Affairs estimates cumulative cost 2022-25 at $22.4B ($15.6B above-benchmark payments, $4.2B admin, $2.7B arbiter fees), which I only saw second-hand. Volume ~1.2M disputes H1 2025 and ~1.4M H2 2025 vs 17,000/yr expected by government.
money_flow: Plans and self-funded employers (via TPAs) pay out-of-network emergency, radiology, anesthesia and hospital-based physicians the offer an arbiter picks, plus a $115 admin fee per party and arbiter fees. Providers and billing intermediaries start ~99.9% of disputes; providers win ~85% with median award ~445% of the plan's in-network benchmark (QPA).
shock: En banc Fifth Circuit (TMA III, 2026-08-11) held the federal QPA rules unlawful on 'ghost rates' and excluded bonus/risk-share payments, so every payer's benchmark methodology is defective and past QPAs may need recomputation; agencies also finalized an IDR Operations Rule in May 2026; insurers are lobbying Congress to overhaul IDR while volume keeps rising 16% half over half.
incumbents: Provider side: PE-backed physician groups (Team Health, SCP Health, Radiology Partners) and contingency billing intermediary HaloMD (~56% of H1 2025 disputes among the top four). Payer side: Claritev (ex-MultiPlan), Zelis, Cotiviti, Fair Health benchmarks, big-carrier in-house teams (UnitedHealthcare, BCBS Texas, Aetna are 57% of disputes).
incumbent_fragility: Payers lose ~85% of disputes and, per physician-group analysis of CMS data, default on roughly 1 in 4 line items; self-funded employers who ultimately fund awards have no defense tooling; the QPA, the legal anchor of the system, was just ruled defective; arbiters are throughput-constrained. Risk: Congress could cap awards and shrink the pool.
funded_startups_already_here: Daffodil Health (payer-side OON pricing/payment integrity, $16.3-16.6M Series A, Flare Capital, ~$20.9M total, 2025-26); Radix Health (software IDR, provider side); Pivotal Health (provider-side IDR, success fee); HaloMD has no disclosed funding I could find. None found for TPA/self-funded-employer IDR defense.
wedge_hints: (a) IDR defense and default-prevention for hundreds of mid-size payers and TPAs with no in-house team; (b) QPA recomputation/audit service after TMA III; (c) pre-IDR negotiation and OON carve-outs for self-funded employers; (d) software for the arbitration entities themselves.
insider_roles: Payer OON/NSA compliance directors, TPA claims-operations VPs, ED and radiology group revenue-cycle directors, IDR-entity reviewers, benefits attorneys.

name: US farmers' spend on equipment repair, maintenance and parts
size_basis: USDA NASS Farm Production Expenditures lists 'farm supplies and repairs' at $24.0B for 2024; repair and maintenance alone was $18B in 2023 (a Senate Agriculture deck citing ERS, not checked against the ERS table). Lower figure used. PIRG separately estimates repair restrictions cost farmers $4.2B a year (advocacy estimate).
money_flow: Farmers and custom operators pay equipment dealers, and a minority independent shops, for parts, labor and diagnostics.
shock: FTC and five states (IL, AZ, MI, MN, WI) settled with Deere on July 8, 2026: 10 years of dealer-equivalent repair tools and software for farmers and independents, including parts pairing, and no retaliation. Deere also agreed in April 2026 to a $99M class settlement for repair payers since Jan 2018. Iowa's House passed a farm right-to-repair bill 70-18 in April 2026.
incumbents: Deere, CNH, AGCO and Kubota dealer networks. One dealer anecdote: parts about 20% of revenue at about 35% margin, service about 10% at about 70% margin.
incumbent_fragility: Business-model conflict: dealer profit is concentrated in service and parts, and the settlement removes the diagnostic-software moat that protected it. Manufacturers earn thin margins on equipment and rely on the aftermarket.
funded_startups_already_here: None found for independent farm repair or parts marketplaces in 2025-26 (searched marketplace, used-parts and right-to-repair startups); an established used-equipment and parts ecosystem exists.
wedge_hints: Dealer-equivalent diagnostics and subscription tools for mixed fleets; mobile technician network; independent shop parts procurement; remanufacturing; technician training; downtime insurance. Actual tool access is unproven until the order is entered and tested.
insider_roles: Independent ag repair shop owners, dealer service managers, custom harvesters, large-farm shop managers, former OEM service engineers.

name: US purchases of power and distribution transformers (utilities, developers, data centers, industrials)
size_basis: Commercial (paid) estimates disagree: MarketsandMarkets $13.76B in 2025 rising to $19.0B by 2030; Arizton $16.5B (2024); GMI $12.2B (2024); narrow-definition outliers $0.7-3.4B. I used the broad definition (~$14B). Cross-check: EEI transmission capex $39.9B (2025 projected) and distribution capex $50.9B (2023), so $14B is plausibly 10-15% of grid capex. Wood Mackenzie: imports ~80% of power-transformer and ~50% of distribution-transformer supply in 2025.
money_flow: Utilities (close to half of distribution-transformer demand in one global forecast), IPPs/developers, data centers and industrials pay manufacturers and electrical distributors; most units are imported.
shock: Section 232 tariffs took effect 2025-08-18 (50% on the non-US steel/aluminum content of transformers). Wood Mackenzie projected 2025 supply deficits of 30% (power) and 10% (distribution); generator step-up lead times passed 160 weeks by Q1 2026; DOE cites >30 months for distribution units; ~40M US distribution transformers are past expected service life; only one US grain-oriented steel producer (Cleveland-Cliffs).
incumbents: Hitachi Energy (>$1B US investment announced 2025-09-04; $457M Virginia large-power-transformer plant broke ground June 2026, operating 2H 2028), Siemens Energy, GE Vernova (closed $5.3B buyout of Prolec GE on 2026-02-02; Prolec 2025 revenue ~$3B), Eaton, Hubbell and regional makers; distributors resell.
incumbent_fragility: New capacity does not arrive until 2027-2028; grain-oriented steel is single-sourced; every utility has custom specs, which blocks standard-unit mass production; utilities hold spares in silos. Manufacturers have cyclical-capex scars and no reason to over-build, so they cannot respond quickly.
funded_startups_already_here: All solid-state-transformer hardware: Heron Power ($140M Series B, Feb 2026, a16z American Dynamism + Breakthrough; $38M Series A in 2025; 40 GW plant, production 2H 2027), DG Matrix ($60M Series A, Feb 2026), Amperesand ($80M Series A, late 2025), Hyperscale Power (EUR 5M seed, Mar 2026). None found funded on repair/refurbishment, spares pooling or spec standardization (searched solid-state and general terms only; 'none found', not 'none exist').
wedge_hints: Transformer repair/rewind and life extension for the ~40M units past service life; mutualized spares pool or group purchasing for ~2,000 public-power utilities and ~800+ co-ops (approximate counts, unverified); standard-spec consortium to aggregate orders into factory slots; condition-monitoring analytics; certified used-transformer marketplace with test data; tariff/import-compliance brokerage. Bottom-up sketch (assumption): a consortium brokering ~$2-3B/yr of co-op and muni purchases at 3-4% is $60-120M.
insider_roles: Utility transformer asset managers; co-op and muni procurement directors; transformer repair-shop owners; distributor reps (Graybar/Wesco type); transformer test labs; NRECA/APPA purchasing staff.

name: Captives, group captives and fronting: corporate premium moving out of the commercial market
geography: Global (Vermont, Delaware, Bermuda, Cayman, Guernsey, Montana; 30+ US states have captive laws)
size_basis: Marsh Benchmarking Report (published 2026-06-01): Marsh-managed captives wrote $79.1B gross written premium in 2025 ($77B in 2024). Swiss Re Institute's older estimate for the whole world was $60-80B, so the true total is at least Marsh's slice. The fee pool inside this (management, fronting, letters of credit, actuarial, reinsurance placement) is much smaller: at an assumed 3-5% it would be $2-4B (hypothesis, unsourced).
money_flow: Corporates and groups of mid-size firms pay premium into their own insurance subsidiary instead of commercial carriers. Fronting carriers issue the policies and charge fees and collateral; managers (Marsh, Aon, WTW, Gallagher/Artex) charge management fees; reinsurers take the excess.
shock: Captives kept growing as commercial pricing fell: Marsh-managed captive premium rose while its commercial price index fell 4% in 2025; Marsh formed 118 new captives in 2025 versus 92 in 2024 and manages about 1,500; third-party-risk captives wrote $4.4B; protected-cell programs grew 47% by premium. Regulatory moves: IRS final rule of 2025-01-14 listing certain 831(b) micro-captive transactions was upheld by one court in March 2026 (CIC Services) and narrowed in April 2026 (Drake Plastics) per conflicting secondary reports; Montana passed a new captive law in May 2025.
incumbents: Marsh Captive Solutions, Aon, WTW, Gallagher/Artex; fronting carriers; group-captive specialists such as Captive Resources (background knowledge).
incumbent_fragility: Conflict of interest: brokers earning commissions on commercial placements run the captives that replace them, so they sell captives to large clients and under-serve mid-size ones. Fronting capacity and letters of credit are costly and slow; domiciles are fragmented; no standard 'captive in a box' exists for a 20-100 unit fleet or contractor group.
funded_startups_already_here: None found with 2023-2026 venture funding for captive management, fronting or group-captive formation. Searched: group captive, fronting fee, captive management, 831(b). One vendor guide says a 20-100 truck fleet needs about $50K-$250K initial capital (marketing estimate).
wedge_hints: 1) Group-captive formation for 20-100 unit fleets, contractors and dealerships with standardized fronting, reinsurance and actuarial work (links to the trucking pool). 2) Captive loss-data benchmarking and feasibility studies as a data asset. 3) White-label cells (protected cell or rent-a-captive) for associations wanting a risk pool without building one. 'Open' on the venture side does not mean easy: heavy capital and regulatory moat.
insider_roles: Captive managers; captive actuaries; Vermont, Delaware, Montana and Bermuda regulators; tax counsel from the 831(b) cases; fronting-carrier underwriters; group-captive agents; CFOs of mid-size trucking and construction firms.

name: US building owners' spend on fire and life-safety inspection, testing, maintenance and monitoring (POTS copper cutover)
size_basis: IBISWorld US fire protection and security system installation contractors $22.1B (2026 label; page text says 2025, year uncertain); fire protection consultants $8.1B. No clean US ITM-only figure exists; my assumption is that recurring ITM, monitoring and code-driven repair is $8-12B of the total. Fragmentation: more than 118,000 privately owned potential acquisition targets (Grata 2026).
money_flow: Commercial building owners pay licensed fire-alarm/sprinkler/extinguisher contractors annual inspection, testing, monitoring and repair contracts mandated by NFPA 25/72 and local fire codes; fire marshals (AHJs) enforce and approve changes.
shock: FCC adopted the Network and Services Modernization order 2026-03-26 (FCC 26-19, WC Dockets 25-208/25-209): ends network-change disclosure filings, 31-day automatic grant for all copper discontinuance applications, blanket grandfathering of legacy copper voice, preempts state/local rules that delay retirement. AT&T stopped taking new copper orders Oct 2025 and targets retiring most copper outside California by end-2029 (vendor trackers). Fire alarm communicators and elevator cab phones on POTS must move to listed cellular/IP communicators. Caveat: the FCC text I read does not name fire alarms; that link is from vendors.
incumbents: Johnson Controls (Tyco), Siemens, Honeywell (panels), Convergint, Securitas, Pye-Barker (57 acquisitions in 2025, 9,000 staff, 47 states), Summit Companies (BlackRock), many PE-owned regionals. Money is annual ITM contracts, monitoring and repair.
incumbent_fragility: Roll-ups are digesting dozens of acquired shops with different paper workflows; licensing is state-by-state; NICET-certified technicians are scarce; inspection reports are still PDFs/paper filed to AHJs; the POTS cutover is a one-time forced retrofit across millions of lines with no standard program, and monitoring contracts carry per-line recurring revenue that incumbents price opaquely.
funded_startups_already_here: Ember Software (ex-Fire Inspect, $10M led by 8VC and Menlo Ventures, Jan 2025); Inspect Point ($28M Mainsail growth equity, Jan 2022); Life Safety Inspection Vault (reported $28.7M, last round Aug 2025, unverified); ServiceTrade and other field-service software. No funded startup found running managed POTS-replacement programs.
wedge_hints: POTS-cutover-as-a-service for multi-site owners (retail chains, school districts, REITs, hospitals): inventory every copper line, replace with listed cellular communicators, file AHJ paperwork, bill monitoring monthly; inspection-report filing network to AHJs (compliance records as data asset); small-commercial sprinkler/extinguisher ITM in metros roll-ups have not reached.
insider_roles: NICET-certified alarm technicians, fire marshals/plan reviewers, central-station operators, telecom managers at national retail chains, insurance loss-control engineers, fire-sprinkler contractors.

name: 340B Drug Pricing Program covered-entity purchases (the spread and the rebate transition)
size_basis: HRSA reports covered entities bought $100B of outpatient drugs in CY2025, up ~22% from $81.4B in CY2024; hospitals ~87%. The contestable money (spread, administration, compliance) is a fraction and I could not source it.
money_flow: Manufacturers sell outpatient drugs at statutory ceiling prices to ~50,000 covered-entity sites; entities bill Medicare and insurers at full rates and keep the spread, increasingly via contract pharmacies run by third-party administrators.
shock: First HRSA rebate pilot was enjoined (D. Maine 2025-12-29) and withdrawn Feb 2026; D.C. Circuit (Novartis v. Kennedy, 2026-07-21) held rebate models lawful only with HHS approval; HRSA published a revised pilot 2026-08-03 effective 2027-01-01 (pay full price, submit claims data, get rebate); AHA sued again 2026-10-09; Congress has competing drafts (Cassidy draft allows rebates or a claims repository, House SECURE 340B Act pauses rebates, Senate SUSTAIN 340B Act moves to a data clearinghouse).
incumbents: Third-party administrators and contract-pharmacy networks (Sentry/Wellpartner, Walgreens, CVS, Verity, Second Sight's 340B ESP) and Kalderos (duplicate-discount and rebate platform).
incumbent_fragility: A rebate model forces hospitals and safety-net clinics to front full price and prove claims-level eligibility: a working-capital and data problem for thin balance sheets and weak data teams. The data standard (clearinghouse vs manufacturer platforms) is unresolved. Risk: outcome splits three ways (rebates, discounts-with-data, pause) and depends on courts and Congress within ~12 months.
funded_startups_already_here: Proximity ($3M seed, Feb 2025, LRVHealth/Commonweal; 340B revenue automation); Pillr Health (Water Street Healthcare Partners investment Jan 2026, size undisclosed; split billing, contract pharmacy, rebate readiness); Kalderos ($7M Series A 2019, $28M Series B 2020, Bain Capital Ventures; no 2023-26 round found).
wedge_hints: Advance financing against 340B rebate receivables; claims-data scrubbing and rebate-submission service for small covered entities and FQHCs; duplicate-discount prevention; a neutral claims clearinghouse if Congress picks that model.
insider_roles: 340B program directors at DSH hospitals and FQHCs, hospital pharmacy directors, manufacturer 340B-integrity leads, TPA compliance staff, health-system treasurers.

name: Indonesia: free-meals programme (MBG) money flowing from BGN through ~27,000 community kitchens (SPPG) to ingredient suppliers
size_basis: 2027 draft budget Rp240T = $15.09B for 60.6M beneficiaries (finance minister, 14 Aug 2026; fetched). 2026 allocation Rp335T (~$21B), Rp153.2T disbursed by end-Sept 2026 (search summary only). Derived: Rp240T / 27,000 kitchens = ~$560k per kitchen per year; ~70% on ingredients (BGN-cited, search summary) = ~$10B/yr of ingredient purchasing. Private capital already sunk in kitchen buildings ~Rp54T.
money_flow: Treasury -> National Nutrition Agency (BGN) -> per-meal payments to ~27,000 privately financed kitchens run by partners (foundations, police-linked groups, businessmen, Kadin) -> ~70% of kitchen budget buys eggs, chicken, rice, vegetables, oil, milk from farmers, traders, cooperatives and village firms (BUMDes; BGN requires purchasing via cooperatives/BUMDes) -> meals to schoolchildren, pregnant women, toddlers.
shock: Aug-Sept 2026 crackdown and re-plumbing: 13 Aug 2026 BGN directive after Berastagi school poisoning (rapid test kits for every kitchen, teachers must reject unfit meals, negligent kitchen heads face dismissal); 12 Sept 2026 BGN announced its own raw-materials marketplace (beef, chicken, eggs, rice, cooking oil, milk) launching late Sept/Oct 2026 with association-vetted sellers; July 2026 pause on new kitchens (partners say up to Rp8.7T investment at risk, ~13,000 kitchens could stall); 1,276 kitchens shut for lacking hygiene certificate (SLHS); a 2026 IPB study found only 44% of sampled kitchens had SLHS. Programme scaled from Jan 2025 to ~57M beneficiaries.
incumbents: No incumbent buyer; the state is a new payer. Money is captured by kitchen partners (many politically or institutionally connected), local wet-market traders, cooperatives and BUMDes, and banks financing kitchens (e.g., BSI Rp181B for 127 kitchens). BGN itself is now building a government commodity marketplace.
incumbent_fragility: BGN is a young agency inspecting 27,000 sites manually with paper reporting; disbursement runs behind budget (~46% spent by end-Sept 2026); policy swings (pauses, new certificates, mandated suppliers) strand kitchen owners who carry bank loans; supply-chain readiness and hygiene compliance are admitted gaps. Rules are being added faster than monitoring capacity exists. Risk to any entrant: the state marketplace and mandated cooperative layer can squeeze private intermediaries, and the programme itself could be cut (2027 draft below 2026 allocation).
funded_startups_already_here: None found for MBG-specific kitchen operations, food safety or procurement (searched English and Indonesian; found no startup names or VC rounds). Government is building its own marketplace. Adjacent Indonesian food-supply-chain startups (Sayurbox, Eden Farm, Chickin) exist from background knowledge, not verified this run.
wedge_hints: (1) Kitchen operating system: menu costing to BGN cost cap, inventory, daily reporting in BGN format, SLHS certificate tracking. (2) Food-safety testing/certification/audit service for kitchens. (3) Working-capital finance for kitchens waiting on BGN disbursements, underwritten on the BGN payment stream. (4) Cold-chain and last-mile ingredient logistics to rural kitchens. (5) Tooling for cooperatives/BUMDes that kitchens are now forced to buy from. Bottom-up: $10B ingredient flow x 1% = $100M but needs near-universal kitchen coverage; SaaS $150/month x 27,000 = $49M at 100% share; testing $1,500/kitchen-year = $40M at 100% share; a $100M path needs 2-3 stacked layers or a balance sheet.
insider_roles: SPPG kitchen heads and nutritionists (ahli gizi), BGN regional coordinators, school principals/UKS officers, village cooperative and BUMDes managers, egg and chicken traders, Puskesmas sanitarians, BPOM/Dinkes inspectors, BSI/BRI kitchen-loan officers.

name: US biofuel producers' purchases of fats, oils and grease feedstock
size_basis: EIA July 2026 monthly feedstock use (million lb): soybean oil 1,687, corn oil 453, canola 330, tallow 771, poultry fat 34, yellow grease/UCO 610, other 101, about 3,990 total, or about 48B lb a year at that run rate. At an assumed $0.50-0.60 a lb (my assumption; current prices not verified) that is about $24-29B.
money_flow: Renewable diesel and biodiesel producers buy soybean oil, tallow, used cooking oil, corn oil and canola oil from crushers, renderers, collectors and importers.
shock: EPA finalized 2026-27 Renewable Fuel Standard volumes in late March 2026 (published Apr 1): 9.07B gallons of biomass-based diesel for 2026, about 60% above 2025 (one source gives 8.95B for 2027, so figures conflict). From 2026 the 45Z credit applies only to North American feedstocks, and from 2028 imported feedstock and fuel get half the RFS value. UCO imports fell 38% year on year (China-origin down 67%), and biofuel's share of US soybean oil use is about 54%, up from 40% two years earlier.
incumbents: Large renderers, crushers (ADM, Bunge, Cargill), thousands of fragmented UCO and grease collectors, and the refiners that buy.
incumbent_fragility: Supply of domestic fats is inelastic in the short run and collection is fragmented, so scarcity rent goes to whoever controls domestic collection and origin documentation; imported-feedstock fraud and certification burdens favor traceable supply.
funded_startups_already_here: None found in feedstock sourcing or traceability (searched renderer, UCO collection and feedstock traceability startups). Capital-heavy at scale, with strong incumbent renderers.
wedge_hints: Grease route-density consolidation with software; origin and carbon-intensity documentation for 45Z and ISCC audits; waste-oil brokerage with North American origin certification; carbon-intensity measurement for soybean growers; offtake for new oilseeds (camelina, carinata, pennycress).
insider_roles: Renderer procurement managers, UCO route collectors, refinery feedstock buyers, RIN traders, carbon-intensity auditors.

name: US heavy-duty (Class 6-8) truck repair, maintenance and parts aftermarket
size_basis: Stale but order-of-magnitude. MacKay & Co: aftermarket parts for Class 6-8 trucks, trailers and chassis were $31.6B in 2019 (forecast $37B by 2024); service labor $58.5B in 2015 and total aftermarket about $107B (Fleet Maintenance citing MacKay; assumes $100/hour and includes in-house fleet work). Verified (ATRI via FleetOwner): repair and maintenance was 21.5 cents per mile in 2025, up 8.6%.
money_flow: Fleets and owner-operators pay OEM dealers, heavy-duty distributors, truck-stop service chains and independent shops for parts, labor and tires; a large share is in-house fleet maintenance. Dealers took 49% of parts purchases and distributors 18% (MacKay 2019).
shock: Section 232 25% tariffs on imported medium and heavy-duty trucks and parts effective Nov 1, 2025 (proclamation Oct 17, 2025; USMCA content relief partial); FreightWaves cites an injector 20-30% pricier than two years ago (anecdote). Carriers keep older trucks longer (C.H. Robinson Oct 2026), driving repair load. ATRI-cited data: 65.5% of shops short-staffed in 2025 with nearly one in five technician slots unfilled (secondary). Record diesel and driver supply cuts squeeze fleet cash.
incumbents: OEM dealer networks, heavy-duty distributors (FleetPride, TruckPro), national service chains (TA, Love's, Pilot), and independent shops (9% of parts purchases). Earn parts margin and labor.
incumbent_fragility: Highly fragmented shops with weak procurement scale, opaque parts pricing, OEM control of fault-code data, and an aging technician workforce. Dealers cannot add technicians fast either, and tariffs hit their parts cost while fleets push back on price.
funded_startups_already_here: Fullbay (shop management software; $23M growth investment from Mainsail / JMI Equity, 2019 vs 2024 dates conflict; says its shops billed $5.04B in 2025, up 68% from 2023). No venture-funded heavy-duty mobile repair, parts marketplace or technician-staffing company found (searched; funded mobile-repair names were light-duty Wrench and RepairSmith). Fleetio-type fleet maintenance software exists but was not re-verified.
wedge_hints: Group purchasing and parts price transparency for independent shops in the tariff era (aftermarket and remanufactured alternatives); technician supply (training, staffing, shared mobile technicians for small fleets); warranty/recall/core recovery for fleets; payments and financing at the shop-to-fleet layer. Bottom-up: Fullbay's $5.04B of annual shop billings is about 5% of the pool; a 1-2% take on a similar flow is $50-100M.
insider_roles: Fleet maintenance directors; independent shop owners and service managers; parts counter managers; FleetPride/TruckPro branch GMs; OEM dealer warranty administrators; tire dealers; diesel technician instructors; owner-operators.

name: Medicaid home- and community-based services (personal care, home care agencies, fiscal intermediaries)
size_basis: CMS: 7.8M HCBS users and $129.4B of Medicaid spending in 2022 (+12.5% y/y); narrower personal-care slice ~$46.4B in 2024 (nearly double 2019) per RealClearInvestigations, New York alone $15.67B.
money_flow: State Medicaid agencies (and managed-LTSS plans) pay thousands of small home care agencies and fiscal-intermediary payroll firms per care hour; most revenue passes through as aide wages.
shock: H.R.1 cuts federal Medicaid by $911B over 2025-34 (KFF), and states historically cut HCBS enrollment and rates; immigration enforcement hits a workforce that is >40% foreign-born for home health aides; New York consolidated ~600 fiscal intermediaries into one statewide FI (PPL) on 2025-04-01 for ~250k consumers; the 80/20 wage pass-through rule (effective ~2030) remains unrescinded.
incumbents: Fiscal intermediaries (PPL, GT Independence, Acumen/Tempus), agency chains (Addus, BrightSpring, Amedisys), software (HHAeXchange for EVV, WellSky, AlayaCare, AxisCare, Axxess, ClearCare).
incumbent_fragility: Thousands of agencies under $20M revenue on thin margins, paid late by states, squeezed by rate cuts and a shrinking labor supply, with EVV compliance burdens and no access to working capital; states are willing to restructure the whole market (New York).
funded_startups_already_here: AlayaCare (C$225M Series D 2021; debt financing Feb 2026), Enzo Health ($20M Series A May 2026, home health/post-acute AI), MochaCare (~$1M accelerator round Mar 2026). No venture-funded Medicaid FI/payroll challenger found.
wedge_hints: Working-capital advances against Medicaid receivables (balance-sheet business); fiscal-intermediary/payroll platform for states that bid statewide FIs after New York; EVV-to-claims reconciliation; caregiver pipeline products for agencies.
insider_roles: Agency owners and administrators, state long-term-care program managers, FI operations VPs, EVV compliance leads, waiver case managers.

name: Utilities' and developers' outsourced transmission and distribution engineering and line-construction contracts
size_basis: Floor figure, annualized from one contractor. Quanta Services' Electric segment booked $7.84B revenue in Q2 2026 (+44% y/y), ~$31B annualized (DERIVED); this excludes MasTec, MYR, Primoris, Henkels & McCoy, Asplundh's utility work and engineering firms. Payer budget: EEI projects $208B of investor-owned-utility capex in 2025 (>$1.1T for 2025-2029), with transmission $39.9B (2025) and distribution $50.9B (2023). Engineering/design is a smaller slice; no sourced engineering share was found (an NYISO independent estimate puts a mixed bucket of mobilization, engineering, permitting, testing, project management and indirects at ~28% of one line's subtotal).
money_flow: IOUs, co-ops, munis, RTOs and data-center/renewable developers pay line contractors (Quanta, MasTec, MYR, Primoris, Henkels) and engineering firms (Burns & McDonnell is ENR's #1 power design firm, Sargent & Lundy #3; also Black & Veatch, POWER Engineers, Ulteig, Kimley-Horn). Utility capex is recovered through rates.
shock: Quanta's Q2 2026 revenue was $9.56B (vs $6.77B a year earlier), total backlog $53.4B, 2026 guidance raised to $39.3-39.7B, and it added ~7,400 employees through four acquisitions in the quarter and July; more meaningful field activity on some newly booked projects is expected from 2H 2027. EEI's capex plan and data-center load growth are the drivers; the lineworker and engineer shortage is widely cited but no 2026 source was found.
incumbents: Quanta, MasTec, MYR on construction; Burns & McDonnell, Sargent & Lundy, Black & Veatch on engineering. They bill by the hour or unit and design still runs on utility-specific standards and desktop tools.
incumbent_fragility: Growth is gated by hiring, not demand; automation reduces billable hours (business-model conflict); every utility's design standards differ; small utilities cannot compete for contractor crews.
funded_startups_already_here: Piq Energy ($5M seed, 2026-07-08; automates interconnection/grid-planning studies), Pearl Street Technologies (acquired by Enverus, Mar 2025), envelio (German; Eversource uses it). Nothing funded found on distribution design, estimating, crew productivity or lineworker workforce.
wedge_hints: Distribution design automation for new-load service requests on utility GIS; estimating and bid tools for line contractors; crew scheduling, materials staging and yard logistics; mutual-assistance storm-staffing marketplace; lineworker apprenticeship and credentialing pipeline (a network/standard asset); outsourced 'engineer-in-a-box' for ~2,000 public-power utilities and ~800+ co-ops (approximate counts, unverified). Bottom-up sketch (assumption): design automation plus engineering-as-a-service for 200 mid-size utilities at $500k each is $100M; a workforce marketplace taking 3% of $30B+ is ~$1B at full share but a thin-margin labor business.
insider_roles: Utility distribution planners and designers; line-construction superintendents; contractor estimators; T&D engineering managers; storm-response coordinators; IBEW/NECA training directors; project-controls managers.

name: US consumer auto-loan interest and fees, with the subprime servicing, collections and repossession layer under stress
size_basis: NY Fed Q2 2026 auto balances $1.713T times an assumed blended APR of roughly 7.5-8% (my assumption; Experian Q1 2026 originations average 6.39% new, 11.43% used, 21.77% deep-subprime used) gives about $130B interest a year. Subprime was 15.75% of Q1 2026 financing; subprime-only slice probably $40-55B (my estimate). Servicing/collections cost not sized from a source.
money_flow: Borrowers pay interest and fees to banks, captives, credit unions, finance companies and buy-here-pay-here dealers. Lenders pay servicers, collection agencies, repo agents and auctions for servicing, recovery and remarketing.
shock: Tricolor Holdings filed Chapter 7 on Sept 10, 2025 (alleged double-pledged collateral); Vervent took over servicing of about 100,000 loans within days. Fitch subprime 60+ day delinquency 6.9% in Jan 2026, reported as a record since the 1990s (vendor-cited; Philadelphia Fed argues it overstates new distress). NY Fed Q2 2026: 3.00% of balances flowed into 90+ day delinquency, most new serious auto delinquencies since 2010. Cox: about 1.73M repossessions in 2024, highest since 2009.
incumbents: Captives and banks (Ally, Capital One, Santander Consumer, Credit Acceptance, Westlake; from memory), independent subprime lenders and BHPH dealers on legacy servicing systems (Megasys-type vendors), collection BPOs paid on recovery, successor servicers such as Vervent.
incumbent_fragility: Independent subprime lenders have thin operations and fail abruptly (Tricolor), forcing emergency servicing transfers. Collection BPOs are paid on recovery, so they have no incentive to prevent default. Legacy servicing systems cannot do channel-level outreach or fast portfolio onboarding. Regulator enforcement pressure that used to fund compliance vendors has eased (my understanding, not sourced).
funded_startups_already_here: Salient ($60M Series A, Jul 2025, loan-servicing AI; Axios Pro headline only, paywalled), Prodigal (AI collections for subprime auto; funding unverified), Vervent (successor servicer; ownership and funding unverified). No funded startup found focused on post-repo recovery, deficiency balances or a standing backup-servicing utility.
wedge_hints: (1) Warm backup and successor servicing for small subprime lenders and ABS issuers (payers: warehouse lenders, ABS investors). (2) Early-intervention and extension programs priced per saved loan, below expected loss avoided (round 1 failed on this price/value test). (3) Post-repossession recovery and remarketing including deficiency balances. $100M revenue is about 0.08% of interest dollars.
insider_roles: BHPH dealer principals, subprime collections managers, repossession agents and forwarders, auction remarketing managers, ABS investors and rating analysts (Fitch, KBRA), consumer-bankruptcy attorneys.

name: Airlines' and lessors' spend on commercial aviation MRO and aftermarket parts
size_basis: Estimates range $83-136B: Precision Aviation Group cites about $97B for 2026 (up from $91B in 2025), Spherical Insights $114B for 2025, Cassel Salpeter $136B for 2025 on a broader scope, Business Research Company $88.7B for 2026. Engine MRO alone about $50.7B in 2026 (Straits Research). Used serviceable material is a small sub-slice at about $6.2B (Business Research Company). I use about $100B.
money_flow: Airlines and lessors pay engine shops, component repair stations, airframe MROs and parts distributors; OEMs capture a large share via long-term power-by-the-hour agreements and proprietary parts.
shock: IATA/Emerton study (Jun 25, 2026): engine MRO bottlenecks are disrupting airlines; GTF-powered groundings peaked at 648 aircraft (28% of the GTF fleet) in March 2025; LEAP shop visits rise from about 600-800 (2025) to over 5,000 a year by 2040; GTF from about 1,000 to over 2,000. Secondary reports: more than 3,500 engines stalled awaiting castings and forgings; overhaul turnaround 180-240 days in 2026 vs 60-90 pre-2019. Tariffs (15% Section 301 on Chinese-origin parts, 25% on certain EU-origin parts per one analysis) raise costs. Airlines keep old aircraft and lease extra ones.
incumbents: OEMs (GE Aerospace, RTX/Pratt & Whitney, Safran/CFM, Rolls-Royce); MROs (Lufthansa Technik, AFI KLM E&M, ST Engineering, StandardAero, AAR, HAECO); parts distributors (Boeing Distribution, AJW, Satair). Earn long-term service agreement revenue, proprietary parts margin and repair labor.
incumbent_fragility: OEMs are constrained by supply of castings and forgings and cannot add shop capacity quickly; IATA and airlines are pushing for fair MRO market access, spare-parts price transparency and more PMA and used-parts channels. Counterfeit-document scandals push buyers toward traceable parts. OEM business models rely on parts exclusivity they cannot give up easily.
funded_startups_already_here: ePlane (B2B aerospace parts and repair marketplace; $9M round led by Marubeni Mar 2024, about $16.5M total then; a Series C reported Feb 2026 by one aggregator, unverified), plus marketplaces fipart, PartPilot, PartsBase, AeroParts Now, Honeywell GoDirect Trade, Locatory. AerSale and AAR are public. No 2025-26 venture rounds found for engine-MRO or PMA-development startups (searched).
wedge_hints: PMA and DER-approved repairs for high-failure rotables on A320/737 families and regional fleets (ATR, E-Jets); engine teardown and module-level used serviceable material trading; traceability and documentation verification for parts transactions; AOG parts logistics and lease-return inspection. $100M is 0.1% of the pool; a USM/PMA business at 10-20% gross margin needs roughly $0.5-1B of throughput, so inventory capital is the constraint, not demand.
insider_roles: Airline MRO procurement and technical services directors; engine shop planners; FAA DERs; USM traders; lessor technical reps (AerCap, SMBC); Part 145 repair-station quality managers; AOG desk coordinators.

name: State Medicaid and SNAP agencies' eligibility and administration spend (work requirements, 6-month redeterminations, SNAP admin cost shift)
geography: US (43 expansion states + DC for Medicaid work requirements; all 50 states for SNAP)
size_basis: Derived. KFF: Medicaid administration is about 4% of total Medicaid spending; applying 4% to roughly $0.9T total spending (my assumption, verify vs CMS-64) gives about $35B. SNAP: USDA impact analysis (cited by CSPI/FRAC) shifts about $16.9B of admin cost from federal to states over FY2027-31 as the federal share drops 50% to 25%, implying total SNAP admin of roughly $13B/yr. Sum about $45-50B, order-of-magnitude. Only a fraction is outsourced to vendors; that share is not sourced.
money_flow: Federal match (generally 50% for admin, higher for some eligibility systems) plus state general funds go to state Medicaid/human-services agencies, which pay systems integrators (Deloitte, Conduent, Gainwell, Maximus, Accenture, GDIT, Optum, Acentra, RedMane, Curam/Merative), county eligibility workers and call-center/mail vendors. Managed-care plans separately pay for member outreach and retention (my inference).
shock: H.R.1 (July 2025) requires 80 hrs/month work or similar activity for Medicaid expansion adults from 2027-01-01 plus six-month renewals; CMS interim final rule issued 2026-06-01 (91 FR 33348), states had to send notices by 2026-08-31 and finish system changes by late 2026; CMS projects about 2.3M fewer enrollees in FY2027 and 3.1-3.3M later. SNAP: federal admin share falls to 25% on 2026-10-01 (about $16.9B shift to states over FY2027-31); from FY2028 states with error rates above 6% share benefit costs.
incumbents: Ten integrators pledged about $600M in discounted/free services to CMS in Jan 2026: Accenture, Acentra Health, Conduent, GDIT, Deloitte, Gainwell, Maximus, Curam by Merative, Optum, RedMane. They earn on long-term state system contracts and per-transaction operations. CMS also offers $200M in Government Efficiency Grants and a free federal toolkit (EMMY) of eligibility-verification APIs.
incumbent_fragility: Hard Jan 2027 deadline against slow state procurement; legacy integrated eligibility systems; political exposure (Senators Wyden, Warren, Sanders, Warnock wrote to Conduent, Deloitte, GDIT, Gainwell about payment structures and error handling); discounts signal pricing pressure. Caution: the free federal EMMY tooling is a public substitute, and states estimated only $3-10M each for work-requirement system changes (about $0.1-0.4B one-time across 43 states, derived), so the real money is recurring operations, not one-time build.
funded_startups_already_here: Fortuna Health (a16z, BoxGroup, YC; navigation/enrollment, Gainwell partner), Develop Health ($14.25M Series A Aug 2025; benefits verification, adjacent), Argyle (consent-based income data marketing to Medicaid verification), Ocrolus (2018 $4M Series A for Medicaid eligibility, precedent). No 2026 round found for a pure work-requirement verification company. Searched: startup raises funding Medicaid work requirements verification. Nonprofit/civic tech (Nava, Code for America) exist from background knowledge, not checked.
wedge_hints: (1) Retention services paid per retained member by managed-care plans (inference: 2.3-3.3M coverage losses at roughly $7k/yr capitation, an assumption, means $16-23B plan revenue at stake); (2) ex parte data-matching feeds (payroll, education, caregiver and medical-frailty exemptions) sold to states or sub-licensed to integrators; (3) notice, mailing and call-center overflow for counties; (4) SNAP payment-error-rate reduction, since states face hard-dollar liability from FY2028; (5) appeals/fair-hearing support.
insider_roles: State Medicaid eligibility policy directors; county eligibility supervisors; SNAP quality-control reviewers; managed-care plan member-engagement/retention executives; integrator program managers (Deloitte, Conduent, Gainwell); benefits legal-aid attorneys; state procurement officers.

name: US homeowners insurance premiums in wildfire-, hail- and hurricane-exposed markets (California cat-model reform, Florida reinsurance reset)
geography: US, concentrated in CA, FL, TX, CO, LA
size_basis: S&P Global Market Intelligence on NAIC data: about $173.1B direct homeowners premium written in 2024 (+13.4%, combined ratio 99.3%); NAIC says 2025 growth slowed, so 173 is a floor. State Farm held about 19.4% of 2024 premium. Figure came via search summary of the S&P article, not read in full.
money_flow: Households (via mortgage escrow) pay carriers and residual plans (CA FAIR Plan, FL Citizens). Carriers pay claims, cat reinsurers, agent commissions and modelers. Residual plans assess the industry when they lose money.
shock: California Sustainable Insurance Strategy lets insurers price with forward-looking wildfire cat models and pass California-only reinsurance costs into rates in exchange for writing in distressed areas (85% of market share). CDI approved the Verisk wildfire model 2025-07-24; Mercury filed the first rate case by 2025-08-15. CDI's Aug 2026 brief: twelve insurer groups have filed under SIS, FAIR Plan growth under 2% in Q2 2026. FAIR Plan has about 668k policies and a roughly 30-35% rate hike for renewals from 2026-10-15 (secondary sources conflict). Opposite pole: Florida Citizens fell from about 1.4M policies (Sept 2023) to 293,772 (May 31, 2026) and June 2026 cat reinsurance fell 15-20%. NAIC: Palisades and Eaton were the costliest wildfires in world history.
incumbents: State Farm, Allstate, Farmers, Progressive, USAA, Chubb, Mercury, CSAA; independent agents; cat modelers Verisk, Moody's RMS, KCC. Carriers earn the spread between premium and modeled loss; modelers license by seat.
incumbent_fragility: State Farm General went to S&P CreditWatch Negative and sought an emergency 17% hike. California is prior-approval, so every change needs a filing and the regulator sets the pace. The 85% writing commitment must now be proven with data. Legacy policy and inspection workflows cannot ingest mitigation evidence at scale.
funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: RockRose Risk ($12.5M Series A, Aug 2026, vertically integrated wildfire mitigation plus insurance, plans to acquire tree-trimming and roofing firms); BurnBot (Mercury strategic investment, May 2026); BirdsEyeView (seven-figure round, Jan 2026, wildfire modeling); Zesty.ai (Series B 2022, CDI-accepted model, no 2026 round found); Kettle (wildfire reinsurance MGA, $25M Series A, older). From background knowledge, not re-verified: Kin, Openly, Hippo, Lemonade, Branch.
wedge_hints: 1) Verified-mitigation evidence layer: SIS forces discounts and published wildfire risk scores, but homeowners must prove work (photos, invoices, IBHS or third-party inspection; State Farm's 2024 version needed a $125 inspection fee) - a registry or inspection-and-repair network carriers accept. 2) FAIR Plan take-out tooling (policy matching, pricing, agent workflow) for the twelve SIS carriers; Florida's nine Citizens take-out approvals Feb-Apr 2026 are the template. 3) Wildfire rebuild and claims logistics (contractor capacity, permits) after Palisades and Eaton. 4) Parametric deductible top-ups sold through MGAs.
insider_roles: CDI rate-filing analysts and carrier actuaries who file SIS cases; independent agents in California WUI zones; wildfire claims adjusters from Palisades/Eaton; FAIR Plan underwriters; Fire Safe Council and mitigation contractors; mortgage servicers' hazard-loss departments; Florida reinsurance brokers.

name: US homeowners-insurer-paid property repair and restoration (claims money flowing to contractors)
size_basis: III (verified): 2025 net premiums earned $152.6B; incurred losses 53.6% of premiums = ~$82B; loss plus LAE 61.1% = ~$93B. ISO 2023: property damage 97.3% of claims (wind/hail 42.5%, water 22.6%, fire 21.6%), so the claim money is overwhelmingly repair/rebuild spend. LA fires alone: CA Dept of Insurance says >$22.4B paid on 42,121 claims (secondary).
money_flow: Insurers pay claim proceeds, often by check jointly payable to homeowner and mortgage servicer (loss draft), which flow to roofers, restoration contractors, GCs and public adjusters; carriers also pay adjusters, TPAs and estimating software. Signers: restoration/roofing contractor owner; servicer loss-draft operations head; carrier claims-ops VP.
shock: Jan 2025 Los Angeles wildfires (largest payout event), plus 2025-26 shift to actual-cash-value/payment-schedule roof settlements. Verisk 2026 roof report (secondary): roof claims fell ~20% in 2025 but average roof replacement hit $17,631 (+33% vs 2021-24). Texas TDI clarified 2026-09-29 that insurers may weigh roof condition.
incumbents: Carriers; Verisk (Xactware/Xactimate) and Cotality for estimating; Sedgwick and Crawford as TPAs/adjusters; restoration franchisors; public adjusters (vendor names other than Sedgwick not re-verified). Mortgage servicers control loss-draft release (Fannie/Freddie thresholds per a Louisiana AG summary: <=$20k to borrower alone, >$20k joint with contractor, licensed contractor at $40k+; verify against Selling Guides). ~60% of owner-occupied homes carry a mortgage (ACS 2022, secondary).
incumbent_fragility: Contractor base is fragmented and cash-constrained; carrier payment rules are changing (ACV roofs, schedules); the servicer loss-draft step is a manual back office. Carriers resist tools that raise payouts, so contractor-side products need to be paid by contractors.
funded_startups_already_here: Rebuild (restoration claims software, $13M Series A Sept 2026 led by Asymmetric Capital Partners; $2.1M seed Jan 2025); NovaData Solutions (carrier-side restoration invoice review, Series A Mar 2024, Activate Venture Partners); Xcelerate (restoration documentation software); T&M Pro (acquired by Sedgwick).
wedge_hints: Contractor cash acceleration against approved claims; recoverable-depreciation holdback recovery on ACV roofs; servicer-side loss-draft disbursement and inspection workflow; contents inventory; post-catastrophe lien and payment tracking.
insider_roles: Restoration estimators and owners, public adjusters, mortgage servicer loss-draft managers, roofing contractor owners, carrier claims-operations leaders.

name: US prison and jail health care (state corrections departments and counties paying contractors)
geography: US (state prisons, county jails, some federal)
size_basis: Derived, state prisons only. Pew: state prison health spending was $8.1B in FY2015 (about a fifth of prison budgets); grown about 3%/yr (my assumption) gives about $11B. Jails and the federal Bureau of Prisons would add more (not sourced; likely several billion). Cross-check: Maryland alone awarded $1.7B for five years of state-prison care, about $340M/yr.
money_flow: State corrections departments and county sheriffs/boards pay contractors fixed or capitated prices per facility; some states run care in-house. One analysis (unverified) says only 14 states still run prison health in-house and 36 outsource at least part.
shock: Wellpath (largest private provider) filed Chapter 11 on 2024-11-12 and emerged 2025-05-12 owned by its lenders; YesCare filed for bankruptcy 2026-05-08 and Polk County, Florida terminated its contract that day (CFG Health Systems took over); Doña Ana County, NM signed a roughly $4.5M emergency contract with Thrive Medical after YesCare missed payroll; Maryland dropped YesCare for Centurion ($1.7B state prisons, $723M pretrial, five years plus two-year option); Shasta County moving to Mediko ($25M/3 yrs); Medicaid reentry (90 days pre-release) waivers starting, with 12 states given CMS planning grants in Jan 2025 (Nevada's $5M for an EHR that can bill Medicaid).
incumbents: Wellpath, Centurion (Centene-linked, ownership unverified), YesCare/Corizon, NaphCare, plus regional firms (Mediko, CFG Health Systems, Thrive). They sell thin-margin fixed-price or capitated facility contracts.
incumbent_fragility: Heavy wrongful-death/civil-rights litigation, debt loads (Wellpath restructured about $550M), repeated payroll failures, and counties left with no bidder. Buyers (sheriffs, county boards) are risk-averse and procurement is slow, which also slows any newcomer.
funded_startups_already_here: none found. Searched: correctional healthcare startup raises funding jail telehealth reentry Medicaid 1115 waiver. Safety Net Connect (eConsult specialty referrals) announced a correctional-health expansion in July 2025 with no round named.
wedge_hints: Off-site specialty and hospital referral management (a major cost driver, not sourced here); Medicaid reentry enrollment and billing infrastructure for states and counties; pharmacy and formulary management; staffing and in-house program support for counties that fire a vendor; EHR plus billing for jails.
insider_roles: Jail health administrators; state DOC health services directors; NCCHC accreditors; county risk managers; correctional nurses and physicians; civil-rights litigators who sue these contractors.

name: US nuclear fleet operating, fuel and capital spend (and the outsourced supplier/services ecosystem behind it)
size_basis: DERIVED. 816 TWh generated in 2024 (World Nuclear Association) x $31.76/MWh total generating cost (NEI/EUCG 2023 dollars: fuel $5.32, capital $7.06, operating $19.38 per MWh) = ~$25.9B; operating cost alone is ~$15.8B. Uses 2023 cost data with 2024 generation; no newer NEI edition was found.
money_flow: About two dozen owner-operators (Constellation, Vistra, Duke, Southern, Dominion, Entergy and others) pay fuel suppliers, O&M labor, outage-services firms (Westinghouse, Framatome, BWXT, Curtiss-Wright, Jacobs, Bechtel and specialists), engineers (Sargent & Lundy is ENR's #1 nuclear-plant design firm), compliance and NRC fees. Hyperscaler PPAs now fund uprates and restarts.
shock: Executive Order 14300 (2025-05-23) sets 18-month limits for new-reactor decisions and 12-month limits for license renewals, with NRC final rules due ~November 2026 and an NRC reorganization. Follow-through: NRC approved TVA's Clinch River BWRX-300 construction permit on 2026-09-29 (14-month review), TerraPower's Natrium permit in March 2026, four DOE pilot test reactors reached criticality by 2026-07-04, and Palisades began fuel loading (~2026-08-31) after repeated slips.
incumbents: Owner-operators' in-house staff plus the OEM/outage-services oligopoly capture the money; documentation, quality assurance (NQA-1) and condition-report workflows are largely manual.
incumbent_fragility: Aging workforce; regulatory documentation (licensing responses, 10 CFR 50.59 screenings, condition reports) is mostly hand-written; very few shops hold nuclear quality certifications, so the new-build and uprate wave hits a supplier base that cannot scale; commercial-grade dedication is slow and expensive. QA sign-offs cannot be waived by software.
funded_startups_already_here: Nuclearn ($10.5M Series A, Sept 2025, Blue Bear; claims >65 reactors; per-reactor annual subscription) and Atomic Canyon ($7M seed, May 2025, Energy Impact Partners; Diablo Canyon customer). Both target documentation/AI search, not supplier qualification, staffing or outage services. Reactor developers (Valar, Aalo, Antares, Deployable Energy) are funded but do not attack fleet spend.
wedge_hints: Nuclear supplier qualification and commercial-grade dedication marketplace; outage workforce staffing and credentialing (radiation-worker portability); counterfeit/suspect-item detection; procurement of nuclear-grade valves and pumps; uprate engineering at scale; restart and decommissioning services; licensing documentation (contested). Bottom-up sketch (assumption): if outsourced services and supplies are ~40% of the pool (~$10B), a staffing/qualification marketplace taking 5% is ~$500M at full share; $100M needs ~20% of that, a stretch without a standard or certification role.
insider_roles: Plant licensing engineers; outage managers; procurement and commercial-grade dedication engineers; NQA-1 lead auditors; radiation protection technicians; fuel reload engineers; former NRC resident inspectors.

name: US federal agencies' spend on management advisory and professional support services (consultants and support contractors)
geography: US federal government (shock concentrated on civilian agencies)
size_basis: Bloomberg Government (Jan 2026, paywalled, secondary): FY2025 management-advisory obligations fell 19% to a five-year low, civilian down one-third to $26B and DoD down 1% to $24B. GAO FY2025 snapshot (total contract commitments ~$793B; professional support services ~$26B at DoD and ~$18B civilian, a narrower category).
money_flow: Agencies pay labor-hour/time-and-materials fees to primes (Booz Allen, Deloitte GPS, Accenture Federal, SAIC, CACI, Leidos) and to small-business subcontractors via GSA schedules and IDIQs.
shock: Feb 2025 GSA memo told agencies to review and justify contracts with the 10 highest-paid consulting firms (>$65B in fees in 2025 and later); Bloomberg reported ~1,700 GSA consulting terminations claiming $4.5B savings, then a second phase pushing outcome-based restructuring ($8.9B immediate savings claimed). Deloitte at least 127 contracts cut or modified, Booz Allen ~61, Accenture at least 30 ($240M).
incumbents: Booz Allen (almost all of ~$11B revenue is public sector), Deloitte Government and Public Services, Accenture Federal (federal ~8% of global revenue FY2024), SAIC, CACI, Leidos; revenue depends on billable headcount.
incumbent_fragility: Labor-hour model conflicts with outcome-based buying and AI productivity; civilian demand down by a third and agencies must defend spend. Counterpoint: DoD contract spend is growing ($491.6B FY2025 vs $445B), so the shock is civilian-only; moats are past performance, set-asides and clearances.
funded_startups_already_here: No funded AI-native delivery firm selling services to federal civilian agencies found. Funded players are software for contractors: NationGraph ($18M Series A, Feb 2026), Vultron ($22M Series A, 2025), Ask Sage ($17M Series A, Dec 2024), Procurement Sciences AI ($10M Series A, 2024). Real competitors are mid-size GovCons with set-aside status; big firms repositioning toward agent delivery.
wedge_hints: Fixed-price, outcome-priced work replacing terminated time-and-materials contracts at civilian agencies (claims backlogs, grants management, FOIA, IT modernization); subcontract slots with primes that must reprice; small-business set-aside entry (status of SBA 8(a)/set-aside programs in 2026 not verified, check). Payer who signs: contracting officer with agency CIO/program office as sponsor.
insider_roles: GSA FAS contracting officers and CORs; agency CFO/CIO staff; capture and pricing leads at primes; small-business subcontractors; OIG and GAO auditors; former DOGE/GSA acquisition staff.

name: German Mittelstand ownership succession: purchase-price flow plus advisory and financing fees
size_basis: Derived: KfW Nachfolge-Monitoring 2025 reports about 109,000 successions a year planned through 2029 at an average intended sale price of about EUR 499,000, giving about EUR 54B (about $62B at 1.15). This is an upper bound: not all are sales and the price is owners' hope. IfM Bonn expects about 37,200 actual handovers a year (reported, unverified), roughly EUR 18B. The capturable fee and financing layer is about 3-8%.
money_flow: Successors pay retiring owners; Steuerberater, M&A boutiques, banks (Sparkassen) and KfW take fees and interest.
shock: KfW Jan 2026: for the first time, planned closures without a successor (about 114,000 a year) exceed succession wishes (about 109,000). More than 2M owners are 55+; 42% of firms planning closure cite bureaucracy (+12 points); employee and management buy-outs are being considered by 28% and 24%.
incumbents: Tax advisers (Steuerberater), Sparkassen and Volksbanken, IHK/HWK succession advisers, M&A boutiques, nexxt-change (free state-backed board), KfW loans.
incumbent_fragility: Free public substitutes price matching at zero; advisers skip sub-EUR 1M deals; information is hidden and valuations are opaque; many firms are too low-earning to sell.
funded_startups_already_here: None found with a 2023-2026 round in Germany. Historical: Carl Finance (EUR 3M, 2019), Valuedesk (EUR 5M, 2024, valuation SaaS), UnternehmerTUM ETA programme (Sept 2025). US analogs now funded: Baton, Rowan, Iconic.
wedge_hints: EBO/MBO financing with KfW and Bürgschaftsbank guarantees; buy-and-hold vehicles for the roughly 114,000 planned closures; Handwerk trades (about 1M firms); valuation benchmarks. A $100M revenue path needs $1.5-3B of transacted value.
insider_roles: Steuerberater, IHK and HWK succession moderators, Sparkasse corporate-client advisers, notaries, business brokers.

name: Clinical laboratory testing (independent, hospital-outreach and reference labs)
size_basis: US clinical lab services ~$99.7B revenue in 2024, projected $122.5B by 2029 (Hyde Park Capital, secondary). Medicare Part B lab spend $8.4B in 2024 per HHS OIG as cited by MarkNtel (secondary), 43% genetic tests. Narrow ~$10B market-research figures are not comparable.
money_flow: Medicare, Medicare Advantage, commercial plans and Medicaid pay labs per test; Medicare's rate is set from a private-payer rate survey under PAMA, so Medicare cuts propagate to billing and contracting.
shock: CMS's preliminary 2027 clinical lab fee schedule (week of 2026-09-25) applies the maximum 15% cut to ~775 tests (~1,200 tests total per ACLA) with more cuts in 2028-29, after Congress delayed cuts a seventh time in the Feb 2026 appropriations act; CMS says it saves ~$1B a year; the RESULTS Act (claims-database rate setting) is pending and analysts expect another delay.
incumbents: Quest and Labcorp (buying hospital outreach labs), thousands of regional and specialty/genetic labs; billing systems XIFIN, Sunquest, Orchard, offshore RCM shops.
incumbent_fragility: Independent labs run thin margins, depend on payer coverage decisions (MolDX) and the PAMA rate, and hospitals are selling outreach labs; billing is legacy or offshore. Risk: Congress may delay cuts again, weakening urgency.
funded_startups_already_here: None found that are lab-specific revenue-cycle companies (general RCM adjacent: Candid Health $120M Series D, Silna Health $27M). Only three searches; low confidence.
wedge_hints: Lab-specific underpayment and denial recovery on contingency; payer-rate benchmarking for labs in the 2025 PAMA data cycle; outreach-lab transition services for health systems.
insider_roles: Independent-lab CFOs and billing managers, hospital outreach-lab directors, MolDX/coverage consultants, lab sales managers.
